answer.answer: Apollo crews carried out EVAs on the Moon to do geological fieldwork and collect samples, with trained geologists like Jack Schmitt spending a combined 22 hours on three excursions [5]. They returned substantial rock collections to Earth — for example Apollo 14 brought back about 94 pounds from the Fra Mauro hills — and NASA established the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility to protect and store those samples for decades [4][2]. Earlier Project Gemini spacewalks helped validate the EVA techniques and procedures later used for surface activity [1]. Taken together, the clips show planned field science, extended surface EVAs, and the retrieval plus long-term curation of lunar rocks — a synthesis no single clip provides on its own [5][4][2][1].

chronology.claim: Project Gemini spacewalks demonstrated EVA capabilities that informed later lunar surface operations.
Apollo 11 achieved the first lunar landing and public attention for lunar surface operations (era label from archive video/scene).
Apollo 14 returned about 94 pounds of lunar rocks from the Fra Mauro region, showing the scale of sample return.
By Apollo 17, trained geologist-astronauts like Jack Schmitt conducted extended fieldwork, totaling many hours outside the spacecraft.

answer.caveats: The archive-era labels come from the items' metadata (e.g., era noted as video/scene) rather than independent chronological verification; the clips do not provide a complete inventory of all surface activities or the full mass of samples from every mission.
